items.title: Global heating will hit at least 1.8C, UN warns, and there are ‘no good outcomes’
items.summary_raw:
But scientists say the world could get back to 1.5C through deep, rapid emissions cuts and removing carbon from the atmosphere

Global heating will reach at least 1.8C under even the most optimistic future, well beyond the Paris agreement goal of 1.5C, according to a UN report that warns every fraction of temperature rise intensifies destructive extreme weather, glacier melt, ecosystem loss, and island and coastal city submersion.

The report by the Nairobi-based UN Environment Programme confirmed overshooting the 1.5C goal inscribed in the landmark Paris agreement of 2015 was now “unavoidable” and, despite some progress in addressing the human-caused climate crisis driven by burning fossil fuels, likely in the next few years.

items.title: Oil Giant Chevron Is Expected To Announce It Will Expand Operations in Venezuela, US Official Says
items.summary_raw:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Oil giant Chevron is expected to soon announce it will expand operations in Venezuela, a U.S. official said Tuesday. The official, who briefed reporters on the expected announcement, said that the company’s officials and Energy Secretary Chris Wright are expected to visit Venezuela on Wednesday where the new investment will be formally unveiled. The official spoke under condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the White House for the call. Chevron is the second-largest U.S. oil company and the only one with a major presence in Venezuela. Chevron did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The announcement comes after the White House confirmed on Monday it is partnering with North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) as part of President Donald Trump ’s push to tap into Venezuela’s oil industry.

The policy required big oil companies to pay $75bn over 25 years for projects to help New York pay for climate mitigation and adaptation.

items.title: Nepal’s glacial collapse foreshadowed a future of climate disaster | Michael Mann
items.summary_raw:
The deluge capped a summer of extreme climate events, from deadly heatwaves to wildfires. We must take action now

For millennia, the high peaks of the Himalayas were held together by an invisible, frozen cement – permafrost and glacial ice that bound ancient rock into seemingly unshakable fortresses. But as the planet continues to warm, this alpine glue is liquefying.

The glacial collapse and deluge in Nepal and Tibet was not a freak weather event; it was the structural failure of a mountain itself, nature’s latest commentary on the deadly consequences of human-caused planetary warming. And it was the exclamation point on a summer of extremes, illustrating with a sole unnatural disaster the apocalyptic future that lies in store if we fail to take dramatic climate action.

items.title: The Nepal and Tibet flood is a warning: melting snow and ice will bring more disasters around the world |  Bill McGuire
items.summary_raw:
In Alaska, the Himalayas, the Andes, Greenland, and perhaps also the Alps, deadly chain reactions are just waiting to be triggered

You may not have felt it, but the earth beneath our feet is getting twitchier, and global heating is to blame. As temperatures surge and climate breakdown accelerates, interactions between climate and geology are becoming ever more apparent – as marked by last week’s horrific events in Nepal and Tibet. items.title: Turkey says roadmap being prepared to expand Mecca defence alliance
items.summary_raw:
Turkey says roadmap being prepared to expand Mecca defence alliance

Turkey is working on a roadmap for other countries to join a joint defence pact established earlier this month with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Monday.

Fidan was speaking at a press conference after the first meeting of a key committee established under what has been described as the “Mecca Defence Alliance”.

The alliance brings together Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, three predominantly Sunni Muslim countries that are also US partners, amid growing regional security concerns.

The three countries signed the defence agreement on 7 August in Mecca, Saudi Arabia. Fidan said work was now under way on a mechanism to allow other countries to join the pact.

items.title: Pentagon signs seven-year deals to boost missile production
items.summary_raw:
Pentagon signs seven-year deals to boost missile production

The US Pentagon said on Monday it had secured seven-year agreements with General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems and Lockheed Martin to increase missile production.

The agreements aim to “increase production quantities and accelerate delivery schedules” for critical missile components used in the THAAD and Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptor programmes, the Pentagon said.

The move comes as demand for US missile defence systems has increased amid escalating conflicts and growing concerns over missile threats in the Middle East and beyond.

items.title: ‘Breakthrough’ as Turkmenistan starts fixing ‘mindboggling’ methane mega-leaks
items.summary_raw:
Secretive state begins repairs on ageing facilities after being revealed as worst country for leaks of potent greenhouse gas

Turkmenistan has started plugging the mega-leaks of methane that spew from its ageing oil and gas facilities, the latest UN data shows, in a move hailed as a breakthrough.

Methane, also called natural or fossil gas, is a potent greenhouse gas. It traps 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide and causes 25% of global heating today. Stopping leaks can be quick and cheap and, because methane breaks down in the atmosphere far quicker than CO2, this has a rapid impact, with some experts calling it the climate “emergency brake”.

items.title: The Nepal floods seem a world away – but make no mistake, climate breakdown will affect us all | Nesrine Malik
items.summary_raw:
Richer countries might have more resources to deal with catastrophe, but this problem grips the entire planet, however much leaders may want to deny it

Climate breakdown is happening on one Earth, but two different worlds. In one, its impacts increasingly encroach on everyday life; longer periods of discomfort and shorter periods of sharp pain. Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice in Nepal that so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.

The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. items.title: Chinese Espionage at British Base in Akrotiri Feared on Cyprus
items.summary_raw:
NICOSIA – British military circles have expressed concerns that facilities at a luxury hotel in eastern Limassol could be used to spy on the British base at Akrotiri according to ANA-MPA. At the center of an exclusive report by The Telegraph is the ultra-luxury casino resort City of Dreams Mediterranean. According to the report, the hotel’s facilities, particularly its upper floors, could be used as an observation point overlooking the British base, according to intelligence and military sources cited by The Telegraph. A representative of City of Dreams Mediterranean categorically rejected the claims, stressing that the property operates exclusively as a tourism and business resort. The report points to the geographical location and height of the 16-story hotel, which have reportedly raised concerns among security officials and RAF personnel. With certain observation equipment, it would potentially be possible to monitor aircraft takeoffs and landings, as well as the movements of officials and military personnel.

items.title: Dead and Missing After Ship Carrying 267 Passengers and Crew Capsizes Off Kyrenia
items.summary_raw:
NICOSIA – A passenger vessel carrying 259 people and eight crew members capsized off the coast of Kyrenia around midday Sunday, August 30  as a rescue operation involving the Turkish-occupied north’s so called coast guard and civil defense teams was underway. According to the illegal Turkish Cypriot Bayrak broadcaster, the passenger catamaran was traveling to the port of Tasucu in Mersin, southern Turkey. The high-speed passenger vessel, operated by Filo Denizcilik, departed from Kyrenia’s tourist harbor and, while several kilometers offshore, began taking on water at the bow. According to available information, the captain attempted to return to port but was unable to do so. The vessel quickly began listing and eventually capsized. The so-called prime minister of the Turkish-occupied north, Unal Ustel, announced that 237 of the 267 people aboard had been rescued, seven were recovered dead and 23 remained missing.

items.title: Flooding devastated swathes of Indiana but response is hampered by politics
items.summary_raw:
Record inundations wrecked homes and took seven lives but Trump has not approved emergency aid and state has cut funds for environmental agencies

It’s been 10 days since the floodwater receded from Cambridge City’s main street and yet signs of disaster are all around.

Abandoned cars, toilets and bathtubs are strewn across parks and side streets on a recent visit to the city. Garages have been lifted from their foundations and moved by the rushing water. Dumpsters up and down the street are overflowing with people’s belongings, with red paint sprayed on homes indicating which houses have been cleared by water rescue teams.

items.title: Araghchi calls for accountability over US use of Japan's airbase to attack Iran
items.summary_raw:
Araghchi calls for accountability over US use of Japan's airbase to attack Iran

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has called on the Japanese public to hold their government accountable over reports that US military assets stationed in Japan were used in operations against Iran.

Speaking to Kyodo News, Araghchi referred to reports that US Air Force F-16 fighter jets deployed from Misawa Air Base to the Middle East took part in operations against Iran.

“The peace-loving people of Japan should ask their government to be held accountable for the crimes committed by the United States,” Araghchi said, arguing that Tokyo bears responsibility for how military facilities and capabilities based in Japan are used.

items.title: Israel to sign $3.6bn defence deal with Greece, its largest ever
items.summary_raw:
Israel to sign $3.6bn defence deal with Greece, its largest ever

Greece is set to sign a $3.6 billion defence deal with Israel on Monday in Tel Aviv, which will provide Athens with an air defence system.

The project, known in Greece as “Achilles Shield”, will become the largest defence export deal in Israel's history, according to Jerusalem Post.

Most of the funds will go to Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, which will supply Greece with David's Sling systems designed to intercept heavy rockets and ballistic missiles, as well as mobile SPYDER systems designed to counter unmanned aerial vehicles and drones, the report said.

Israel Aerospace Industries will provide the Barak MX system, which is designed to defend against aircraft and missiles.

items.title: PM Mitsotakis Urges Voters to Judge Government on Progress Made
items.summary_raw:
The lignite phase-out was inevitable, Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said on Saturday in an interview with e-ptolemeos.gr, adding that the challenge now is to complete the process under conditions of a just development transition. He identified private investment, PPC’s new investment programme, renewable energy sources, infrastructure and the use of funding from the Just Development Transition Programme as key drivers. The Greek premier also referred to investment in healthcare, district heating, tourism and livestock farming, as well as the need to create a new productive model capable of keeping people in the region.

The post PM Mitsotakis Urges Voters to Judge Government on Progress Made appeared first on The National Herald.

items.title: The U.S. has transferred large quantities of missiles and air-defense systems to the Middle East for the Iran war, leaving some stockpiles in Europe and Asia at critically low leve…
items.summary_raw: The U.S. has transferred large quantities of missiles and air-defense systems to the Middle East for the Iran war, leaving some stockpiles in Europe and Asia at critically low levels, according to U.S. officials.  Patriot, ATACMS and other precision weapons have been heavily depleted, while THAAD interceptors and counterdrone systems have also been shifted to the region. Replenishing inventories could take years.  The shortages are forcing U.S. commanders to adjust contingency plans and have raised concerns about Washington’s ability to respond simultaneously to a potential Chinese attack on Taiwan or a Russian threat to NATO.  Source: WSJ

Under the reported arrangement, Venezuela’s interim government granted the venture a 100-year concession to operate the affected oil fields. The U.S. government would control 55% of the venture, through a combination of equity and the ability to acquire oil at cost.  The Trump administration says the arrangement could bring nearly $100 billion in private investment, increase U.S. oil supplies and eventually reduce energy prices. The administration also says the deal comes at no cost to U.S. taxpayers.  The agreement covers roughly one-fifth of Venezuela’s more than 300 billion barrels of proven reserves. Venezuela has the world's largest proven oil reserves, but production has been constrained for years by underinvestment, deteriorating infrastructure, sanctions and the nationalization of foreign-owned assets. items.title: Far-Right British Provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos Arrested by US Immigration Enforcement
items.summary_raw:
U.S. Immigration officials arrested controversial British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos on Thursday in New Orleans, according to the Department of Homeland Security. Immigration officials announced on Friday that Yiannopoulos was arrested at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport and accused him of overstaying after entering the United States legally in May 2019 through New York City. An immigration judge issued a final order of removal on July 22 after Yiannopoulos failed to show up for his immigration hearing, a DHS spokesperson wrote in an email. “He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” a spokesperson for DHS wrote in an emailed statement. ICE’s online detainee locator doesn’t say where Yiannopoulos is being held but directs family and legal representatives to the agency’s office in Alexandria, Louisiana, a deportation hub for international flights.

More than 400 endangered animal and plant species could face accelerated extinction after the Donald Trump administration’s decision to rescind a rule that has protected old-growth forests for more than two decades.

According to a new report from the Center for Biological Diversity, the rollback of the Bill Clinton-era “roadless rule” could put 7.4m acres (3m hectares) of endangered-species habitat and nearly 1,800 miles (2,900km) of protected rivers and streams at risk, while opening more than 45m acres of national forests to roads, drilling and logging.

An official presidential decision in Turkey has granted visa exemptions to Syrians holding diplomatic passports, the Official Gazette reported.

items.title: Trump Administration Starts Building Border Wall Project in Arizona Over Tribe’s Objections
items.summary_raw:
PHOENIX (AP) — The Trump administration has begun work on a project to build a stretch of border wall in southern Arizona along part of a Native American tribe’s reservation, pushing ahead with one of its signature projects despite protests from the tribe. U.S. Customs and Border Protection says the area is a dangerous smuggling route and that building the wall will close a longstanding security gap. But members of the Tohono O'odham Nation, whose membership spans both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border, have accused the administration of trespassing and say the construction will damage land sacred to the tribe. The wall segment is part of a $46 billion effort by the Trump administration to fill the border with 30-foot (9-meter) steel bollard walls, vehicle barriers, and technology designed to stop undocumented immigration and smuggling.

The post Trump Administration Starts Building Border Wall Project in Arizona Over Tribe’s Objections appeared first on The National Herald.

A series of strong El Niño climatic patterns in recent decades, such as the “Godzilla” event currently brewing that is set to warp weather around the world, have been supercharged by the broader overheating of the planet caused by the burning of fossil fuels, a major new study has found.

El Niño is a naturally occurring phenomenon, taking place every two to seven years, when the waters of the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean heat up, causing a cascade of impacts around the world. The latest developing El Niño, set to peak later this year, is set to be the strongest in living memory and has been informally dubbed a “Godzilla” event.

Thousands of people in Nepal and Tibet are in desperate need of emergency assistance following Wednesday’s disaster. With 360 people confirmed dead, more than 1,300 others are still missing as search and rescue operations continue. The precise sequence of events linking glacier collapse to flash floods is yet to be confirmed. But there is no doubting the enormous destructive power of the brown torrent that can be seen on video clips surging down the steeply sided Himalayan valleys, sweeping away everyone and everything in its path.

Testimony from survivors about terrifying near-escapes and losses is reminiscent of previous disasters, including the 2004 tsunami. items.title: Germany's far-right AfD pledged to remove refugee and disabled children from mainstream schools if it wins the Saxony-Anhalt regional election on September 6.  The party's manifest…
items.summary_raw: Germany's far-right AfD pledged to remove refugee and disabled children from mainstream schools if it wins the Saxony-Anhalt regional election on September 6.  The party's manifesto calls the "inclusion experiment failed" and says refugee children should be educated separately "to reinforce the message that their stay in Germany is only temporary."   Islamic education would not be offered as "Islam is not part of Germany."  The AfD also plans to expand Russian language teaching and reinstate school exchanges with Russia, citing cultural ties from the East German era.  The AfD leads polls heading into the election.   It would need over 40% to form the first wholly AfD government in German history.

items.title: Japan killed 14,000 bears after a rise in deadly attacks on people – but is a cull the answer?
items.summary_raw:
Bears killed 13 people in Japan last year, as a lack of forest foods increased human-wildlife conflict. But the controversial cull in response has raised concerns with conservationists

Every summer, millions of people escape the heat and humidity of Tokyo by heading to the tranquil resort town of Karuizawa in Japan’s Nagano prefecture – just an hour by bullet train from the capital. Here, at the foot of Mount Asama, visitors stroll bamboo-lined pathways, cycle in verdant highlands, and practise the wellness ritual of shinrin-yoku, bathing among the cool hinoki forests. It would be the ideal nature retreat – if it wasn’t for the bears.

From June to August, bears often move close to Karuizawa, feeding on the mulberries, ants, leaves and cherry blossoms that grow near the town. Unlike nuts, these foods are low in calories, spurring the bears to seek out further sustenance. “They’re more likely to get close to residential spaces to see what they can find,” says Amelia Hiorns, a British zoologist who previously worked with Picchio Wildlife Research Centre in the town. “This combines with the busiest season for tourists.”

items.title: Iran’s nuclear chief says attacked nuclear sites not secure for IAEA inspection
items.summary_raw:
Iran’s nuclear chief says attacked nuclear sites not secure for IAEA inspection

Iran’s nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami said on Wednesday that the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) would not be able to inspect the country's nuclear sites that have suffered attacks in recent months until it develops a specific inspection protocol for such sites and their security is ensured, adding that Iran is still in a wartime situation, in comments carried by Iran’s IRNA news agency.

Eslami said that Trump's threats to bomb the alleged secret Iranian nuclear site show the IAEA are pawns of the US and Israel, and accused the countries of pressuring the IAEA for an inspection.

items.title: Trump Has Submitted Civil Nuclear Agreement With Saudi Arabia to Congress for Review
items.summary_raw: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump has submitted to Congress for review an agreement with Saudi Arabia aimed at bolstering the kingdom's civilian nuclear program, but continues to insist that it won't move forward if Saudi Arabia doesn't normalize relations with Israel, according to a Trump administration official. The classified document was submitted to Capitol Hill on Monday as required by the Atomic Energy Act, according to the administration official, a congressional aide, and two others familiar with the matter. All four spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly on the classified matter. The agreement was signedlast month in Washington by U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright and his Saudi counterpart. But the next day, Trump announced he was requiring the Saudis to normalize relations with Israel through the Abraham Accords as part of the pact — raising doubts that the agreement would come to fruition. Neither the administration official nor the others familiar with the matter would comment on whether Trump's call for the Saudis to join the accords is detailed in the classified document submitted for the congressional review.<

items.title: Groups sue Trump’s EPA over fast-track approval of toxic datacenter chemicals
items.summary_raw:
Exposure to two compounds approved can result in ‘sudden death’ and range of other serious health risks, lawsuit warns

The Trump administration has approved two new datacenter chemicals to which exposure can result in “sudden death” and a range of other serious health risks, like cancer, eye corrosion, neurological damage and reproductive harm, a new lawsuit warns.

The two compounds approved by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) for import and immediate use in facilities across the US are photoacid generators that also appear to be Pfas “forever chemicals”, though it is unclear because much of the EPA documents are redacted. Some Pfas are commonly used in the production of semiconductors.

This article was amended on 26 August 2026. A previous version said the EPA concedes that the chemicals present an “unreasonable risk” to workers. It has been updated to say the chemicals may present an unreasonable risk.

items.title: France is pushing to limit Ukraine's ability to buy non-European military equipment with EU loan money, seeking to steer the €60 billion defense portion of the EU's €90 billion sup…
items.summary_raw: France is pushing to limit Ukraine's ability to buy non-European military equipment with EU loan money, seeking to steer the €60 billion defense portion of the EU's €90 billion support package toward European and French producers.  Ukraine has secured two exemptions so far: one for Chinese drone components and another for US Patriot interceptor missiles.   France wants these exemptions to be temporary, with European suppliers replacing foreign ones as production ramps up.  Nine EU countries including Germany, Sweden, and Poland pushed back, calling for Ukraine to have "maximum flexibility to procure the equipment it urgently needs."  France has a clear commercial interest: its Franco-Italian SAMP/T system is Europe's closest alternative to the US Patriot.  Source: Euronews

The war has crippled Qatar’s LNG lifeline, with damage at Ras Laffan and severe disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz. Qatar is reported to have lost roughly $24 billion in gas sales during the major disruption.

Doha has responded with deep budget cuts, cutting some government spending by 30% and overseas aid by roughly 85%.
